review.summary:
I found no defect in the change that alters the artifact's play or contradicts its main claims. I worked in C:/Users/garus/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Disk-D-Programming-CG-cg-contest-code-royale/e5f4d102-26bd-4f74-986e-7960068e5e9a/scratchpad/recheck/adversarial (called $W below). The repository and build/submit/Player.java (sha256 5bace689...) are unchanged; git status matches the starting snapshot.

- The warm-up works only on copies and shares no mutable state with the real bot. In class-load logs from 5 full games (4 on JDK 17, 1 on JBR 25.0.4), every lambda, LambdaForm and Player$ class loads on turn 0.
- The sha256 is the same with autocrlf=true and with autocrlf=false.
- The ProcessBot/Referee timing is correct as Referee uses it.

All findings are low:
1. procCheck exits 0 when no game was compared (sameAsCurrent=0/0). With the new fallback, a MainBot exception no longer counts as a kill.
2. Params with non-ASCII digits pass validation. FileMerger then deletes the classes and fails while writing, which leaves the old Player.java in place.
3. Six changed behaviours are not caught by any test, and the CR-strip test only works on a CRLF checkout.
4. The fallback prints the stack trace before the answer, and a few paths still exit without output.
5. Items 5-9 are informational (latent issues and measurement biases).

Tests: 28/28 pass.

findings.title: procCheck exits 0 when no game was compared, and the new fallback hides bot exceptions from its kill counter
findings.evidence: ProcessCheck.java:48 compares a game only if the opponent had no timeout or error in either run. ProcessCheck.java:62 exits 1 only on timeouts, kills or differences, and nothing requires compared > 0. A run against a silent opponent prints 'procCheck vs proc:java -version: games=2 wins=2 timeouts=0 kills=0 sameAsCurrent=0/0 maxFirst=111.5ms maxLater=0.0ms' and exits 0. In that run the artifact only played turn 0. Separately, CGRunner.java:43-50 now turns a MainBot exception into WAIT/TRAIN, so Referee no longer records a kill. Only the line comparison can catch it, and that comparison is skipped in exactly the games where the opponent failed. The stack trace then goes only to the inherited console stderr.
findings.suggested_fix: Fail unless compared == games, or report the skipped games and require a minimum. Capture the artifact's stderr in ProcessBot and fail on any stack trace.

findings.title: FileMerger: non-ASCII digits in params pass validation, then the classes are deleted and the old Player.java is kept
findings.evidence: merge() validates params with Params.apply (FileMerger.java:81). The ASCII check (FileMerger.java:87-90) only scans the source files, and the params are inserted afterwards (FileMerger.java:113). Integer.parseInt and Long.parseLong (Params.java:37-38) accept Unicode digits, so 'MAX_TOWERS=３' applies as MAX_TOWERS=3. main() then deletes build/submit/classes (FileMerger.java:46-51), and Files.writeString(..., US_ASCII) (FileMerger.java:52) throws UnmappableCharacterException. Before: sha256 5bace689, 12 classes. After: the same old Player.java with PARAMS="" and 0 classes. This breaks the Javadoc claim 'Checks run before anything is written'. It can be triggered from `./gradlew submit -Pparams=...` in a UTF-8 Linux/macOS shell. On Windows the ANSI code page turns the digit into '?', which Params rejects. More generally, any failed merge check keeps the previous artifact (by design), and BotFactory 'submit' and bench would use it without warning.
findings.repro: In $W/eol/wt-lf (a copy with build/submit already built): java -cp "$W/tools/classes;$W/work/build/classes/java/main" cr.submit.MergeProbe MAX_TOWERS=FW3. Source: $W/tools/src/cr/submit/MergeProbe.java; it replaces FW3 with U+FF13 and calls FileMerger.main.
findings.suggested_fix: Run firstNonAscii on the final merged text, or on params, before touching build/submit. Write to a temp directory and move Player.java and the classes into place only after the compile succeeds.

findings.title: Six changed behaviours have no test, and FileMergerTest's CR check depends on the checkout
findings.evidence: Mutation runs in $W/work. I applied these 6 together and all 28 tests still pass: M5 removes the non-ASCII check from merge(); M9 removes the warm-up deadline; M10 removes the try/catch around play(); M11 reverts Referee dt to dequeue time; M12 makes ProcessCheck.firstDifference always return -1, which would make procCheck pass falsely; M13 sets start = System.nanoTime(). M4 (no CR strip) fails FileMergerTest (FileMergerTest.java:15) only because MainBot, Physics and Protocol happen to be CRLF in this checkout. On an all-LF copy of the same sources FileMergerTest passes, so a CI checkout with autocrlf=false would not notice the regression. firstNonAsciiFindsTheCharacter tests the helper, not that merge() calls it. The mutations that are caught are listed under checks_passed.
findings.repro: Snippets in $W/mut (M*.old/M*.new), applied with python -I $W/tools/mutate.py. Then ./gradlew --no-daemon -q --offline test [--tests <class>] in $W/work. Logs: $W/mut/*.log, $W/mut/gap.log, $W/mut/M4lf.log.
findings.suggested_fix: Test merge() on temp files that contain CRLF and a non-ASCII character. Unit-test firstDifference, artifactParams and the play() fallback with a bot that throws. Add a test with a deadline already past (kinds == 0) and a Referee or DelayedEcho test that checks dt is about the arrival time.

findings.title: The fallback prints the stack trace before the answer, and some paths still exit without output
findings.evidence: CGRunner.java:46-47 calls t.printStackTrace() before the println calls at CGRunner.java:51-52. On the first exception, 6 JDK classes load in that turn: IndexOutOfBoundsException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, Throwable$PrintStreamOrWriter, Throwable$WrappedPrintStream, IdentityHashMap and IdentityHashMap$KeySet ($W/cl/probe-7.log). The answer took 1.17 ms on this machine, and the next turn was normal. If printStackTrace itself throws (for example out of memory), the Throwable escapes main with no output. RuntimeExceptions from readInit/readTurn (25 sites, more than 400 creeps; known IO-L2) are still uncaught. MainBot never threw on valid input in any run, so this only matters if there is a bug.
findings.suggested_fix: Print WAIT/TRAIN and flush first, then print the trace inside its own try/catch(Throwable). Do the same in the warm-up catch.

findings.title: Informational: the warm-up cap is measured from the first token of turn 0, not from process start
findings.evidence: The deadline is turnStartNanos + 300 ms (CGRunner.java:34, 38). turnStartNanos is taken after JVM start, class loading and readInit, and the deadline is checked only before each copy (CGRunner.java:70). If CG counts JVM start-up in the 1000 ms (unknown), the cap does not bound the total. In practice the warm-up took 34-55 ms in fresh JVMs here under every flag set I tried, so the cap is far from binding.
findings.suggested_fix: Optional: record the time at main() entry and use min(turnStart + 300 ms, mainStart + about 500 ms).

findings.title: Informational: the throw-away bot shares the real Params and never gets init()
findings.evidence: CGRunner.java:38 and 68 pass the same Params instance to the warm-up bot, and bot.init() is never called on it. Nothing leaks today. MainBot only reads p.BARRACKS, p.INCOME_TARGET and p.MAX_TOWERS, has no static fields and does not override init. In WarmFuzz, warm-up before every turn left the commands unchanged. A future bot that keeps an RNG in Params, uses static caches or builds tables in init() could have its real play changed, or its warm-up fail inside the catch. CGRunnerTest would catch an exception there, but not a silent state change.
findings.repro: Code reading of CGRunner.java:67-99 and MainBot.java.
findings.suggested_fix: Use new MainBot(params.copy()) and call init on it with a copy of the state.

findings.title: Informational: state.turn is now correct, but the build-conflict parity depends on the seat, which the reader discards
findings.evidence: state.turn equals Rules' s.turn at every input (RulesTest.java:305-319, and 12,702 inputs from both seats in WarmFuzz). However, Rules.java:64 (skip = s.turn % 2) refers to the global seats, while the reader's state always has 'me' as player 0. A future bot on the second seat that simulated with Rules would give the build conflict to the wrong player. The seat can be derived from the global unit order in the input (Protocol.turnInput) or from the start corner, but InputReader does not keep it. No current code simulates.
findings.repro: Code reading of Rules.java:61-64, Protocol.java:47-63 and InputReader.java:64-101.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the seat in InputReader on turn 0 (from the owner field of the first queen line) before any bot runs Rules on its own state.

findings.title: Informational: ProcessBot's arrival times are stamped late and the check does not reject earlier lines
findings.evidence: The reader thread takes the stamp after BufferedReader.readLine returns (ProcessBot.java:59). If that thread is delayed past the deadline, an answer that arrived on time is refused. That is a strict bias under CPU load; the old code had the opposite bias. readLine (ProcessBot.java:81-87) does not reject lines that arrived before the input was sent. In my probe a leftover line from a timed-out turn was accepted on the next call with arrival - t1 = -401.9 ms, which would give a negative dt. Through Referee this needs a bot that prints more than 2 lines, or play continuing after a timeout. Neither happens: a timeout ends the game, and the artifact prints exactly 2 lines.
findings.suggested_fix: Optional: clear queued lines in send(), or refuse lines stamped before t0. Keep timing gates on an idle machine.

findings.title: Informational: FileMerger deletes lone CRs and sorts files in an OS-dependent order
findings.evidence: FileMerger.java:86 calls replace("\r", ""), which deletes a lone CR. Java treats a lone CR as a line terminator, so deleting it could pull the next line into a // comment. A scan found no lone CRs in src today. FileMerger.java:71 sorts Path objects, which compare case-insensitively on Windows and case-sensitively on Linux. The current file names sort the same way on both, but a future pair such as IO.java and InputReader.java would merge in a different order, so the sha256 would differ between operating systems.
findings.repro: python -I scan in the run log (loneCR 0 for every file in src); code reading of FileMerger.java:71 and 86.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace only "\r\n" and reject any remaining CR. Sort by the forward-slash relative path string.

not_checked: CodinGame itself: its JDK 21 (only 17.0.12 and JBR 25.0.4 are installed here), whether the 1000 ms limit includes JVM start-up, single-core or affinity behaviour, and how the IDE handles the pasted file.
Linux: there is no WSL, so the claim that the hash is the same across operating systems rests on code reading (ADV-9) and has not been tested.
By instruction I ran no procCheck series, benchmarks or latency percentiles. All timings are single short runs on a shared laptop while another agent was measuring.
An OOM inside printStackTrace, and the effect of the warm-up on JIT or deoptimisation: code reading only.

The 140/140 procCheck result and the maxLater figures from the task: not rerun. My own process-vs-current evidence is 5 games plus 2 small ProcessCheck runs (the silent opponent and the negative control).

timing.summary:
Latency lens. The new artifact (sha256 5bace689…) removes the turn-1 and first-MOVE stall in every configuration I measured, and no other turn got slower.

**Stall gone.** On the slowest core (LP E-core lp12, mask 0x1000), JDK 17, 120 paired games, turn 1 went from 33.9 ms p50 (max 48.9) to 0.75 ms (max 1.13). On the same core with JBR 25, the first MOVE went from 46.3 ms p50 (max 78.7) to 0.47 ms (max 0.88). The new variant had 0 turns over 25 ms anywhere. The old one had 182 turns over 25 ms and 5 over 50 ms on lp12 with JDK 17, and 11 over 50 ms with JBR 25.

findings.evidence:

With JVM start on the pinned core counted, the new turn-0 maximum was 807 ms over 120 LP E-core games (old 715 ms) and 716 ms on the E-core.

One instrumented game (I1, seed 3008, seat 1, new) took 1384 ms. The bot first read input 1227 ms after the send, so the JVM stalled during start-up; the sampler showed lp12 only 39% busy, so the process was blocked rather than computing. Its warm-up took 157 ms. Old's maximum over all runs is 715 ms.

The deadline is start + WARM_UP_MS, where start = turnStartNanos is taken after the first token of turn 0 (Player.java:423, 1254, 1273, 1277). It therefore does not bound JVM start or init parsing. Whether CodinGame's 1000 ms budget includes JVM start is unknown.
findings.repro: In the work dir: `bash tools/run2.sh I1 I2 I3` (or `X1` for -Xshare:off), then `python -I tools/turn0split.py results/i_lp12_jdk17_v01.csv results/i_lp5_jdk17_v01.csv results/i_all_jdk17_v01.csv`, then `python -I tools/summary.py "lp12=results/lp12_jdk17_v01.csv,results/r_lp12_jdk17_v01.csv"`.
findings.suggested_fix: Not needed for the stall. For a firmer turn-0 bound on unknown hardware, count the warm-up deadline from JVM start, or lower WARM_UP_MS to about 200 ms; that still covers the 177 ms worst case measured on the slowest core.

findings.title: Pre-existing JIT compile bursts at fixed turns cost 8-20 ms on one slow core, the same in old and new
findings.evidence:
On one core, both variants have spikes at three points. The cause comes from the D1 JIT log (results/attrib_lp12.txt):
- Turns 24-26: C2 compile of Player$InputReader::nextInt (Player.java:392); the tier-3 version is made not entrant.
- Turn 127: about 22 C1 compiles of the println path (BufferedWriter.flushBuffer, PrintStream.println, StreamEncoder...).
- Turn 191: PrintStream.writeln, StreamEncoder.write and others. The two println calls are at Player.java:1290-1291.

New's maximum later turn: 20.25 ms (LP E-core, JDK 17), 17.52 ms (LP E-core, JBR 25), 13.26 ms (E-core). On the P-core, one isolated 20.72 ms turn (turn 59) had 0.09 ms in old at the same turn; this looks like hyperthread-sibling noise. Paired differences are centred on zero, so the change neither adds nor removes these spikes.
findings.repro: `bash tools/run2.sh D1` then `python -I tools/attrib.py results/diag_lp12_jdk17.csv`. The top5 lists of `python -I tools/analyze2.py results/r_lp12_jdk17_v01.csv` show the turns.
findings.suggested_fix: Optional. At 20 ms or less against 50 ms no action is needed. If wanted, the turn-0 warm-up could also push nextInt and the println path past their compile thresholds.

findings.title: With JVM start on the slow core, the old artifact had real turns over 50 ms (not seen in the original RT-1 runs); the new artifact has none
findings.evidence:
LP E-core, JDK 17 (B1+R1): old had a turn over 50 ms in 5 of 120 games, all on turn 2 (51.0-58.7 ms). Each followed a turn 1 above the 40 ms budget: the bot printed e.g. 'SLOW turn 1 47ms' (results/lp12_jdk17_v01.csv.err/old_s3012_p1.txt).

In the D1 log, that turn-2 window loads 13 LambdaForm$MH classes, which is the string-concatenation bootstrap of the old SLOW message (Player-b267ba0d.java:1270).

JBR 25, LP E-core (R6): old first-MOVE turns reached 78.7 ms, with 11 turns over 50 ms.

New: 0 turns over 25 ms. Its SLOW message uses StringBuilder (Player.java:1294) and is never triggered.
findings.suggested_fix: None: fixed by the warm-up plus the StringBuilder message. Note for the record: the RT-1 statement that no JDK 17 turn reached 50 ms holds only when the JVM starts unpinned.

not_checked: JDK 21, CodinGame's current Java, is not installed. JDK 17.0.12 and JBR 25.0.4 bracket it, and both show the same picture.

CodinGame's real environment was not measured: Linux, container CPU quota, CPU model, and whether the 1000 ms first-turn budget includes JVM start. Here 'pre' pinning counts JVM start, which is pessimistic.
Idle time between turns was not tested. The harness sends the next input immediately; real games have opponent and referee time, which can only help background JIT finish.
No formal confidence intervals. The bootstrap-turn effects are 30-60x. Later-turn claims rest on paired per-turn differences over 10k+ turns per configuration.

Run quality: B3/B4 ran under the other agent's Gradle (2.2-3.7 cores); the quiet re-runs R3/R4 are the reference. B2 may have been affected near its end. R1 had a foreign Gradle for its last ~10 s, and B5 at its start.

Coverage limits: the boss (process) opponent was run on all CPUs only, P-core and no-CDS runs have 30 games each, and memory limits were not tested. The 1384 ms outlier is put down to a JVM start-up stall from sampler evidence; I did not trace the OS cause.

findings.title: procCheck's sameAsCurrent only catches differences on paths the games exercise, and it compares builds of the same sources
findings.evidence:
This is a limitation of the check, not a defect in the artifact.

I patched a copy of the artifact and ran ProcessCheck against v01 from C:/Users/garus/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Disk-D-Programming-CG-cg-contest-code-royale/e5f4d102-26bd-4f74-986e-7960068e5e9a/scratchpad/recheck/legality-scale/control (output in out/proccheck-positive-control.txt):
- INCOME_TARGET 10->6 (Player.java:1093): 8 of 10 games differed and the run exited 1, so the check works.
- MAX_TOWERS 4->3 (Player.java:1095): passed 10/10 on seeds 5000-5004 and was caught in only 3 of 100 games on seeds 5000-5049.

The reference side is in-process 'current' built from the same sources (ProcessCheck.java:29, 37, 50). The check therefore proves that merging, CGRunner and InputReader do not change the bot's play on the decisions the games reach. It does not test MainBot's logic. The 400/400 here plus the 720/720 chaos comparison are strong for this change, because the warm-up is isolated by construction. A rarely exercised difference could still pass a 20-50 game procCheck.
findings.repro: In <ws>/control, run sed 's/MAX_TOWERS = 4;/MAX_TOWERS = 3;/' on the artifact, then `javac -encoding US-ASCII -d build/submit/classes build/submit/Player.java`, then `java -cp "<ws>/tree/build/classes/java/main;<ws>/tree/build/resources/main" cr.runner.ProcessCheck v01 5 5000` (passes 10/10) and the same with `v01 50 5000` (97/100).
